coverage: All twelve sections, stored as nineteen reading units, including the source notes in both English editions. Named thinkers, historical, literary and religious references; identified people in miracle examples; and the speakers in the staged conversation. No conjectural identities for generic thought-experiment people or school-name adjectives.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: The Roman orator and philosophical writer, also called Tully.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: The Greek philosopher whose work ranges across logic, ethics and the natural world.

entities.name: Jean de La Bruyère
entities.body: The French writer known for his portraits of human character.

entities.name: Nicolas Malebranche
entities.body: The French philosopher associated with the view that God directly causes events.

entities.name: Joseph Addison
entities.body: The English essayist used as an example of accessible philosophical writing.

entities.name: John Locke
entities.body: The English philosopher whose account of ideas Hume repeatedly examines.

entities.name: Adam
entities.body: The first man in the biblical creation story, imagined here reasoning without previous experience.

entities.name: Euclid
entities.body: The ancient Greek mathematician whose geometry supplies examples of demonstration.

entities.name: Epictetus
entities.body: The Stoic philosopher named in the discussion of philosophy and everyday life.

entities.name: Tiberius
entities.body: The Roman emperor used as a historical example of tyranny.

entities.name: Nero
entities.body: The Roman emperor cited alongside Tiberius in the argument about experience.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher associated with the Academy.

entities.name: Speusippus
entities.body: Plato’s nephew and successor as head of the Academy.

entities.name: Xenocrates
entities.body: The Greek philosopher who led the Academy after Speusippus.

entities.name: Polemo
entities.body: The philosopher who succeeded Xenocrates at the Academy.

entities.name: Scipio Aemilianus
entities.body: The Roman statesman and general recalled in Cicero’s quotation about memorable places.

entities.name: Cato the Elder
entities.body: The Roman statesman and censor remembered in the Latin quotation from Cicero.

entities.name: Gaius Laelius
entities.body: The Roman statesman associated with Scipio Aemilianus, named in Cicero’s quotation.

entities.name: Isaac Newton
entities.body: The English mathematician and natural philosopher whose account of motion Hume discusses.

entities.name: René Descartes
entities.body: The French philosopher discussed in relation to causation and systematic doubt.

entities.name: Samuel Clarke
entities.body: The English philosopher and theologian named in the note on causal power.

entities.name: Ralph Cudworth
entities.body: The English philosopher and theologian cited alongside Locke and Clarke.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: The ancient Greek physician invoked in comparing human and natural history.

entities.name: Polybius
entities.body: The Greek historian whose accounts of human conduct Hume recommends studying.

entities.name: Tacitus
entities.body: The Roman historian cited both on human conduct and on reported miracles.

entities.name: Quintus Curtius
entities.body: The Roman historian of Alexander the Great.

entities.name: Alexander the Great
entities.body: The Macedonian king and conqueror whose extraordinary exploits are discussed.

entities.name: John Tillotson
entities.body: The English archbishop whose argument about testimony opens the discussion of miracles.

entities.name: Cato the Younger
entities.body: The Roman statesman whose reputation for truthfulness supplies Hume’s example about testimony.

entities.name: Plutarch
entities.body: The ancient Greek biographer cited as a source of historical testimony.

entities.name: Demosthenes
entities.body: The Athenian orator used as a comparison for religious eloquence.

entities.name: Alexander of Abonoteichus
entities.body: The religious impostor described by Lucian, used in Hume’s discussion of miracle reports.

entities.name: Lucian
entities.body: The Greek satirist whose account exposes Alexander’s religious imposture.

entities.name: Marcus Aurelius
entities.body: The Roman emperor and philosopher mentioned in the examples about religion and philosophy.

entities.name: Livy
entities.body: The Roman historian, also called Titus Livius, whose reports of prodigies Hume discusses.

entities.name: Muhammad
entities.body: The prophet of Islam, named in comparing religious miracle traditions.

entities.name: Vespasian
entities.body: The Roman emperor at the center of Tacitus’s account of alleged healing miracles.

entities.name: Demetrius Poliorcetes
entities.body: The Macedonian ruler mentioned as accepting divine honors.

entities.name: Suetonius
entities.body: The Roman biographer cited in the note on Vespasian.

entities.name: Cardinal de Retz
entities.body: The French churchman and politician who recounts the alleged healing at Saragossa.

entities.name: Abbé Pâris
entities.body: The French Jansenist deacon whose tomb became the focus of reported cures.

entities.name: Montgeron
entities.body: The French judicial official who published evidence for the Jansenist miracle claims.

entities.name: Cardinal Noailles
entities.body: The archbishop of Paris under whose authority evidence for the cures was examined.

entities.name: Mademoiselle le Franc
entities.body: The woman whose reported cure became a disputed Jansenist miracle case.

entities.name: Hérault
entities.body: The Paris police official charged with investigating and discrediting the reported cures.

entities.name: Mademoiselle Thibaut
entities.body: The woman examined by De Sylva in another disputed healing case.

entities.name: De Sylva
entities.body: The physician sent to examine Mademoiselle Thibaut.

entities.name: Saint Paul
entities.body: The Christian apostle invoked in the comparison with miraculous prison releases.

entities.name: Duc de Châtillon
entities.body: The French nobleman who testified about a reported cure of his servant.

entities.name: Blaise Pascal
entities.body: The French mathematician and religious writer whose niece is discussed in the miracle examples.

entities.name: Jean Racine
entities.body: The French dramatist and historian of Port-Royal cited on the reported cure.

entities.name: Antoine Arnauld
entities.body: The French Jansenist theologian named among Port-Royal’s influential writers.

entities.name: Pierre Nicole
entities.body: The French moralist and theologian associated with Port-Royal.

entities.name: Herodotus
entities.body: The ancient Greek historian whose marvelous accounts are compared with later religious histories.

entities.name: Juan de Mariana
entities.body: The Spanish historian and Jesuit cited among Christian writers of marvelous accounts.

entities.name: Bede
entities.body: The English monk and historian cited alongside Mariana.

entities.name: Lucretius
entities.body: The Roman poet cited for the Latin phrase about an eager audience.

entities.name: Elizabeth I
entities.body: The English queen used in an explicitly imaginary example of death and resurrection.

entities.name: Francis Bacon
entities.body: The English philosopher quoted on scrutinizing reports of extraordinary events.

entities.name: Protagoras
entities.body: The Greek sophist mentioned in the discussion of religious persecution.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher whose trial and death enter the discussion of tolerance.

entities.name: Epicurus
entities.body: The Greek philosopher whose position the skeptical friend defends in an imagined speech.

entities.name: Cassius Dio
entities.body: The Roman historian cited in the note on imperial support for philosophy.

entities.name: Zeuxis
entities.body: The ancient Greek painter used in an example about what a work reveals of its maker.

entities.name: George Berkeley
entities.body: The Irish philosopher whose arguments about perception Hume discusses.

entities.name: Pierre Bayle
entities.body: The French philosopher and critic mentioned in the discussion of skepticism.

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.body: The Roman statesman used in an example distinguishing existence from mathematical truth.

entities.name: Venus
entities.body: The Roman goddess of love, mentioned as a subject for painting.

entities.name: Helen of Troy
entities.body: The famously beautiful woman of Greek legend, mentioned as a subject for painting.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine creator whose existence and causal role are examined in the philosophical arguments.

entities.name: Jesus Christ
entities.body: The central figure of Christianity, called the Savior in the discussion of miracle testimony.

entities.name: The Holy Spirit
entities.body: The divine Spirit invoked in the discussion of Christian belief and testimony.

entities.name: Serapis
entities.body: The Egyptian and Greek god invoked in the account of Vespasian’s alleged cures.

entities.name: The Devil
entities.body: The evil spiritual being invoked in an explanation offered for the disputed miracles.

entities.name: Jupiter
entities.body: The Roman chief god used in the imagined argument about divine providence.

entities.name: Gabriel
entities.body: The angel used alongside Caesar in an example about claims of existence.

entities.name: The Indian prince
entities.body: The unnamed prince in the anecdote about finding reports of frost hard to believe.

entities.name: The blind man in Alexandria
entities.body: The man said to have been healed by Vespasian’s spittle.

entities.name: The lame man in Alexandria
entities.body: The man said to have been healed by Vespasian’s touch.

entities.name: The Saragossa doorkeeper
entities.body: The cathedral doorkeeper whose supposedly restored leg is described by Cardinal de Retz.

entities.name: Noailles’s successor
entities.body: The later archbishop of Paris asked to examine the Jansenist miracle claims.

entities.name: Châtillon’s servant
entities.body: The servant whose reported recovery is supported by his employer’s testimony.

entities.name: Marguerite Périer
entities.body: Pascal’s niece, whose reported healing at Port-Royal is discussed.

entities.name: The bishop of Tournay
entities.body: The churchman cited as using the Port-Royal healing account against unbelief.

entities.name: The queen-regent of France
entities.body: The French regent who sends her physician to examine the Port-Royal cure.

entities.name: The queen-regent’s physician
entities.body: The doctor sent to investigate the reported cure at Port-Royal.

entities.name: The king of France
entities.body: The French king whose edict closes access to the abbé’s tomb.

entities.name: The skeptical friend
entities.body: Hume’s unnamed conversation partner in the discussion of providence and a future life.

entities.name: Hume, in the conversation
entities.body: The author speaking with his skeptical friend in the staged philosophical conversation.
